title: THE SIN WAS SHOCKING. BUT WHAT THE CHURCH DID ABOUT IT WAS EVEN WORSE.
paragraphs: THE SIN WAS SHOCKING. BUT WHAT THE CHURCH DID ABOUT IT WAS EVEN WORSE.

He was sleeping with his father’s wife. The congregation knew. And instead of mourning, they were proud. Nearly 2,000 years later, Paul's warning still confronts every church that has confused the love of Jesus with permission to keep living in sin.
“It is reported commonly that there is fornication among you, and such fornication as is not so much as named among the Gentiles, that one should have his father's wife.” — 1 Corinthians 5:1 (KJV)
Imagine walking into church on a Sunday morning.
The worship is beautiful. The congregation is singing. People are raising their hands, quoting Scripture, greeting one another with smiles.
Everything looks holy.
But somewhere among the worshipers sits a man involved in a sexual relationship with his own father's wife.
And people know.
The leaders know. The congregation knows. The scandal is no longer a secret.
Yet somehow, the church has learned to live with it.
The music continues. The gatherings continue. The religious conversations continue.
And nobody seems willing to confront what God has already condemned.
Then a letter arrives from the apostle Paul.
And within a few sentences, the atmosphere changes.
Because Paul does not congratulate the church for being accepting.
He asks why they are not grieving.
“And ye are puffed up, and have not rather mourned.” — 1 Corinthians 5:2 (KJV)
Read that again.
The scandal was not merely what one man was doing.
The scandal was what an entire congregation had become comfortable tolerating.
And before we point our fingers at Corinth, there is a question we cannot escape.
What happens when the people who are supposed to represent Jesus become more afraid of confronting sin than of grieving the heart of God?
This is not simply an ancient story about sexual immorality.
It is a mirror.
And sometimes the most uncomfortable thing about Scripture is discovering that the person standing inside the mirror looks disturbingly familiar.
Long before Paul wrote to Corinth, God had already spoken clearly about this kind of relationship.
Leviticus 18:8 declares:
“The nakedness of thy father's wife shalt thou not uncover: it is thy father's nakedness.” (KJV)
In the Hebrew text, the command begins:
עֶרְוַת אֵשֶׁת־אָבִיךָ לֹא תְגַלֵּה
ʿErvat ʾeshet-ʾavikha lo tegalleh.
Literally, the expression means, “The nakedness of your father's wife you shall not uncover.”
The Hebrew expression “uncover nakedness” is a recognized biblical idiom for prohibited sexual relations in this legal context.
This was not merely a warning against embarrassing one's family.
It was a direct prohibition against sexual intimacy with a father's wife.
The expression includes a stepmother, not only a biological mother. Scripture distinguishes this prohibition from the separate prohibition concerning one's mother in Leviticus 18:7.
The moral boundary was clear.
The relationship violated God's revealed command and dishonored the family relationship that the law was protecting.
Centuries later, the church in Corinth was facing precisely this kind of offense.
Paul wrote in Greek:
Ὅλως ἀκούεται ἐν ὑμῖν πορνεία
Holōs akouetai en hymin porneia.
The sense is, “Sexual immorality is actually being reported among you.”
The word πορνεία (porneia) refers broadly to sexual immorality. Its precise application is determined by the context.
Here, Paul immediately identifies the offense:
ὥστε γυναῖκά τινα τοῦ πατρὸς ἔχειν
Hōste gynaika tina tou patros echein.
The phrase describes a man having his father's wife.
Paul does not specify whether the father was still alive, whether the woman was legally married to him at that moment, or how the relationship began.
We should not invent details Scripture does not provide.
But we do know this.
The man was involved in a relationship that violated a clear biblical sexual boundary, and the church was failing to respond appropriately.
Paul was astonished that such immorality existed among people who confessed the name of Christ.
But his next words are especially revealing.
He did not simply say, “How could this man do such a thing?”
He said, in effect, “How can you be proud when you should be mourning?”
The Greek word translated “puffed up” is πεφυσιωμένοι (pephysiōmenoi), from a verb associated with being inflated or arrogant.
The church was exhibiting pride when the situation demanded grief and humility.
We are not told exactly what the Corinthians were proud of. Perhaps they imagined themselves spiritually mature. Perhaps their broader divisions and arrogance had blinded them.
But we must be careful not to claim that they were celebrating the immoral relationship itself. Paul does not explicitly say that.
What he does say is devastating enough.
They were proud when they should have been brokenhearted.
And this is where the story stops feeling ancient.
Because we know what it is like to protect appearances.
We know what it means to smile in public while something is rotting in private.
We know how easily people learn to excuse what they once would have confessed.
A compromise begins quietly.
A message that should never have been sent.
A relationship that should never have developed.
A secret that requires another secret to survive.
A conscience that once trembled before God slowly becomes accustomed to the very thing that used to bring conviction.
And then comes the most dangerous sentence a person can speak to himself:
“It's not that serious anymore.”
But sin does not become holy because we have become familiar with it.
And a church does not become more Christlike by pretending that God's commandments no longer matter.
There is a difference between welcoming a sinner to hear the Gospel and affirming a believer's decision to remain unrepentant.
Jesus welcomed sinners.
He ate with tax collectors. He spoke with the morally disgraced. He extended mercy to people religious society had written off.
But His mercy was never an invitation to make peace with darkness.
In John 8:11, Jesus tells the woman brought before Him:
“Neither do I condemn thee: go, and sin no more.” (KJV)
Mercy and a call to holiness were not enemies in the ministry of Jesus.
They belonged together.
He did not demand that sinners repair themselves before approaching Him.
He came to save sinners.
But He also came to transform them.

And if our version of Christianity offers forgiveness without repentance, comfort without truth, and belonging without any call to discipleship, we must ask whether we are faithfully representing the Jesus revealed in Scripture.
Because the Gospel is not permission to remain enslaved.
It is the announcement that through Jesus Christ, sinners can be forgiven, reconciled to God, and made new.
Paul understood this.
That is why his response in 1 Corinthians 5 was so serious.
He instructed the congregation to remove the unrepentant man from its fellowship.
The language is severe. Paul even speaks of delivering the man to Satan.
But we cannot ignore the purpose Paul gives.
“That the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord Jesus.” — 1 Corinthians 5:5 (KJV)
The objective was not entertainment.
Not humiliation.
Not revenge.
Not the satisfaction of watching a fallen person suffer.
The stated objective was ultimately redemptive.
The church was to take sin seriously because the man's spiritual condition mattered.
And the holiness of the congregation mattered.
Paul continued with an image his readers would understand:
“Know ye not that a little leaven leaveneth the whole lump?” — 1 Corinthians 5:6 (KJV)
A small amount of leaven works through an entire batch of dough.
His warning was that tolerated, unrepentant sin could corrupt the life of the community.
Not because every struggling Christian must be expelled.
Not because the church should become a gathering of people who pretend to be perfect.
But because openly persistent, serious sin among those professing faith cannot simply be treated as spiritually harmless.
There is an enormous difference between a believer who is fighting temptation, confessing failure, and seeking restoration, and someone who insists that repentance is unnecessary.
The first needs encouragement, patient discipleship, and grace.
The second needs loving, truthful confrontation.
Both need Jesus.
And both must be treated with dignity.
Biblical church discipline is never a license for spiritual abuse, public spectacle, coercion, or protecting powerful people while punishing the vulnerable.
Where abuse, exploitation, or criminal wrongdoing is involved, safeguarding people and reporting to appropriate authorities must not be replaced by an internal religious process.
The woman in Corinth is not described as a church member, and Paul does not explain her circumstances. We should not presume her motives, consent, or responsibility beyond what the passage tells us.
His direct instructions concern the man and the congregation's responsibility toward a professing insider.
And that distinction matters.
Because Paul explicitly refuses to make the church responsible for policing every person outside its fellowship.
He writes:
The church must not demand that unbelievers live as though they have already surrendered to Christ.
Its responsibility is to proclaim the Gospel, practice holiness, and exercise appropriate accountability within its own community.
That should make every Christian think.
We can spend hours condemning the darkness outside the church while refusing to address the darkness we have allowed inside our own hearts.
We can debate the sins of society while refusing to confess the sins we hide behind religious language.
We can become experts at identifying what is wrong with everyone else.
And strangers to repentance ourselves.
Maybe the Corinthian man is not the person in this story who most resembles us.
Maybe it is the congregation.
The people who knew.
The people who continued.
The people who had grown accustomed to something that should have moved them to tears.
And if that possibility makes you uncomfortable, perhaps it is worth sitting with the discomfort instead of rushing past it.
Because conviction is not always an enemy.
Sometimes it is mercy interrupting the slow destruction of a soul.
Consider Peter.
He promised loyalty to Jesus.
He believed he would stand firm.
Yet when fear came, he denied knowing the Lord three times.
Then the rooster crowed.
Luke 22:61 tells us that Jesus turned and looked at Peter.
Imagine that moment.
The sound of the rooster.
The memory of his own confident promises.
The terrible realization that he had done exactly what Jesus said he would do.
And then the eyes of the Savior.
Peter went out and wept bitterly.
But Peter's failure was not the end of his story.
After the resurrection, Jesus restored him and entrusted him with the responsibility of caring for His sheep, as John 21:15–19 records.
The same disciple who had publicly denied Jesus was graciously restored to serve Him.
That is not cheap grace.
That is the astonishing mercy of a risen Savior.
And perhaps someone reading this knows what Peter's tears feel like.
You remember when prayer came naturally.
When opening your Bible felt like meeting someone you loved.
When your conscience was tender.
When you could not imagine becoming comfortable with the thing you are now struggling to surrender.
But something happened.
You became tired.
You became lonely.
You were wounded.
You made a compromise.
Then another.
And somewhere along the way, shame convinced you that returning to God would be harder than continuing to hide.
So you learned to perform Christianity.
You know the songs.
You know when to say amen.
You know how to post encouraging verses.
You know how to look spiritually strong.
But there are nights when the room becomes quiet and you wonder whether God still wants anything to do with you.
Listen carefully.
The blood of Jesus is not weaker than the sin you are ashamed to confess.
First John 1:9 says:
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (KJV)
That promise does not make sin harmless.
It makes repentance possible without despair.
You do not need to pretend that evil was good.
You do not need to rewrite God's Word to make your choices comfortable.
You do not need to convince yourself that the Holy Spirit has stopped caring about your life.
You can come into the light.
You can confess.
You can turn.
You can seek help.
You can begin taking the difficult, practical steps that repentance sometimes requires.
And you can trust the Savior who died and rose again to receive those who come to Him in faith.
But there is another detail in Paul's letter that we must not miss.
After addressing the sin in Corinth, Paul points the church toward Passover.
“For even Christ our passover is sacrificed for us.” — 1 Corinthians 5:7 (KJV)
There it is.
The center of the entire confrontation.
Jesus Christ.
Not moral superiority.
Not religious reputation.
Not the pleasure of exposing someone else's disgrace.
Christ, our Passover Lamb.
The One who gave Himself for sinners.
The One whose sacrifice makes forgiveness possible.
The One whose resurrection announces that sin and death do not have the final word.
Paul's command to remove the old leaven is grounded in what Christ has already accomplished.
Holiness is not the price by which we purchase salvation.
It is the fitting response of those who belong to the Savior.
We do not repent to make the cross sufficient.
We repent because the crucified and risen Christ is sufficient, and His grace calls us out of the darkness.
Titus 2:11–12 teaches that God's saving grace also trains us to reject ungodliness and live godly lives.
Grace is not merely pardon for yesterday.
It is also God's transforming work in us today.
And this is where the Corinthian story becomes even more moving.
In 2 Corinthians 2:6–8, Paul speaks of someone who has been disciplined by the majority and now needs forgiveness, comfort, and reaffirmed love.
Many interpreters have connected that individual with the man from 1 Corinthians 5.
Others caution that the identification is uncertain because Paul does not explicitly name him or identify the offense.
We should respect that uncertainty.
But regardless of whether the passages concern the same person, the principle is unmistakable.
Paul did not believe church discipline should become permanent rejection when repentance and restoration were appropriate.
He warned that excessive sorrow could overwhelm a person.
He called believers to reaffirm love.
Do you see the beauty of that?
The same apostle who insisted that the church must not ignore serious sin also insisted that the church must not withhold comfort and forgiveness from someone who needed restoration.
Truth without love becomes cruelty.
Love without truth becomes compromise.
But truth and love, faithfully held together under the lordship of Jesus Christ, can become instruments of healing.
That is the heart of the Gospel.
Not pretending the scandal never happened.
Not excusing what God has forbidden.
Not reducing a person forever to the worst thing he has done.
But proclaiming that repentance and forgiveness are possible because Jesus Christ died for sinners and rose from the dead.
Not because sin was insignificant.
But because the Savior is greater.
Maybe you are reading this while carrying a secret.
Maybe your marriage is suffering because of choices you have refused to confront.
Maybe you have been involved in a relationship you know you need to leave.
Maybe pornography has become a private prison.
Maybe bitterness has lived in your heart for so long that you now call it discernment.
Maybe your struggle has nothing to do with sexual sin.
Maybe it is dishonesty, pride, envy, greed, unforgiveness, or the exhausting need to appear spiritually superior.
Or perhaps you have been deeply wounded by the hypocrisy of Christians who preached holiness while concealing wrongdoing.
Your wounds matter.
And no one should use this passage to silence victims, conceal abuse, or demand that wounded people return to unsafe situations.
Jesus is not honored by protecting a religious institution at the expense of the vulnerable.
He is honored when His people walk in truth, justice, humility, repentance, and love.
Whatever brought you here, the invitation of the Gospel remains.
Come to Christ.
Not with a carefully edited version of your life.
Not with a religious performance.
Not with an argument explaining why your particular sin should be exempt from God's Word.
Come with the truth.
Come with the grief.
Come with the exhaustion.
Come with the confession you have been afraid to speak.
Jesus said in John 6:37:
“Him that cometh to me I will in no wise cast out.” (KJV)
What a promise.
The One who knows the truth about you is the very One who invites you to come.
And if you are already a believer, remember that repentance is not something you graduate from.
It remains part of the Christian life.
The mature Christian is not the person who has learned to conceal every weakness.
It is the person who continues to bring his life into the light of God's Word and depend upon the grace of Christ.
That includes churches.
A congregation can have excellent preaching, beautiful worship, active ministries, and impressive attendance while still needing to repent.
No church is above correction.
No pastor is above accountability.
No ministry is too important to be truthful.
No reputation is worth sacrificing the integrity of the Gospel.
And no sinner who genuinely turns to Christ should be treated as though redemption is impossible.
Perhaps that is why this ancient letter still feels so painfully current.
It forces us to ask whether we love Jesus enough to receive His correction, not merely His comfort.
Whether we care about souls enough to speak truth with gentleness.
Whether we believe in grace enough to welcome genuine repentance.
And whether we are willing to let the Word of God examine us before we use it to examine everybody else.
If this message has exposed something you have been hiding, you do not have to explain your private struggle publicly.
And if Christ has restored you after a season of failure, consider sharing a testimony of His mercy. Your words may encourage someone who has begun to believe that change is impossible.
Do not underestimate what an honest testimony can do.
Somewhere, someone is reading Scripture with a heart full of shame.
Someone is wondering whether it is too late to come home.
Someone has mistaken conviction for rejection.
Someone needs to hear that Jesus does not call us to hide our sin, but to bring it into the light where His grace can meet us.
If a particular person came to mind while you were reading, consider sending this article privately with kindness rather than using it as a public accusation.
Because faith needs more than a moment of emotion.
It needs roots.
It needs the Word.
It needs prayer, fellowship, accountability, and continued growth in the knowledge of Jesus Christ.
Those free resources matter deeply to our mission.
But sustaining and expanding that work also requires practical support.
And you cannot purchase His favor.
Salvation is by grace through faith, not through financial contributions, as Ephesians 2:8–9 teaches.
But Scripture also honors willing generosity in support of Gospel work.
Paul wrote:
“God loveth a cheerful giver.” — 2 Corinthians 9:7 (KJV)
That is the kind of support we want.
Not pressured.
Not purchased through guilt.
Not offered out of fear that God will be disappointed if you cannot afford it.
But freely given, from a grateful heart, by those who believe in the mission and have the means to help.
It is helping make more Scripture-centered content and discipleship resources available to people who need them.
You can still read, pray, share, comment, invite others, and make use of the free resources.
Your spiritual worth is not measured by your ability to give money.
We are grateful for every sincere way people participate in spreading the Gospel.
Because the mission is not to build a community around a payment.
It is to point people toward a Person.
Jesus Christ.
The crucified Savior.
The risen Lord.
The One who calls sinners to repentance, offers forgiveness through His blood, and transforms lives by His grace.
And that brings us back to Corinth.
Back to the congregation.
Back to the man whose conduct could no longer be ignored.
Back to Paul's painful question.
Why were they proud when they should have mourned?
The answer is not given in full.
But the warning remains.
When a church loses its capacity to grieve over sin, it is in danger of losing its capacity to understand grace.
Because grace only becomes astonishing when we understand what we have been forgiven.
The cross does not tell us that sin was harmless.
It tells us that sin was so serious that the Son of God gave Himself to redeem sinners.
And the resurrection tells us that the story does not have to end in shame.
So do not walk away from this article merely thinking about the sins of another person.
Ask the harder question.
“Lord, where have I become comfortable with what You are calling me to surrender?”
Then listen.
Open His Word.
Confess what needs to be confessed.
Seek wise, trustworthy help where it is needed.
Make restitution where appropriate.
Turn away from what is destroying you.
And keep your eyes on Jesus.
Not because repentance earns His love.
But because His grace is too precious to treat as permission to remain in chains.
The church in Corinth needed correction.
Peter needed restoration.
And every one of us needs the mercy of Christ.
Some of us need to stop hiding.
Some need to stop pretending.
Some need to stop condemning people whom God is calling us to help restore.
And some need to remember that the Savior who calls us to holiness is also the Savior who welcomes the repentant home.
If there is one sentence I hope remains with you long after you close this article, it is this:
The sin you keep defending may be the very prison Jesus is calling you to leave—and the grace you are afraid to receive may be the beginning of your freedom.
